transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-04-02
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Avery (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Liam (AtlasPay Eng Lead), Priya (ML Infra), Tom (Security), Nina (Product)
---
Summary:
Customer running payment conversational assistant, needs strict moderation for PII/fraud while keeping latency sub-350ms p95. Want to understand where to place safety filters (pre-token, in-runtime, post-gen async) and how that interacts with KV cache, batching, and quantization on their private VPC deployment.
Topics:
- Inline token-level filters vs post-generation classifiers
- Cost/latency of synchronous moderation at 95/99th percentiles
- KV cache effects (warm vs cold) and prefix caching interplay with moderation
- Batching strategies when moderation is in the path
- Quantization impacts on false-positive/negative rates for classifiers on-device
- VPC/on-prem constraints and options for safe pathing
Action items noted above.
---
Transcript:
[00:00] Avery (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call, and then Maya is gonna go through the perf tradeoffs with safety filters.
[00:18] Liam (AtlasPay): Yep, hi all, Liam here. We are pretty time-boxed today, two big questions: where do we run our safety checks so we don't blow latency, and what happens to the KV cache and batching if we move filters inline.
[00:30] Maya (SE): Cool, great. So high level: three placement options we see in the field — pre-filtering (light heuristics before hitting model), inline token-level filters inside the generation loop, and post-generation async classification or rerank. Each has different perf and detection tradeoffs.
[00:50] Tom (Security): Can you define "token-level filter inside the loop"? I just want to be clear on what triggers look like.
[00:58] Maya (SE): Yeah, basically as the model generates tokens we run a small classifier on the prefix or token logits to detect violations and either block/continue, or trigger a safe decode. That can be very precise because you see partial context, but it is blocking — it sits on the hot path.
[01:16] Priya (ML Infra): Blocking how bad? If we have a 300ms generation, what is the extra delta?
[01:22] Maya (SE): It depends on implementation. If you do a lightweight linear classifier on logits on the same GPU, delta can be tiny, like 5–15ms per check. If you call out to a separate process or CPU-bound model, the tail can blow up — 50–200ms. Also depends on whether you run it every token or every N tokens.
[01:41] Avery (AE): Important callout: our runtime supports running small safety kernels on the same device path; we can co-locate filter kernels to avoid IPC if desired, reduces p95 impact. But that has resource contention with generation and may reduce throughput.
[01:57] Liam: Right — we don't want throughput to collapse during peak payment windows. What about post-generation?
[02:05] Maya: Post-gen async classification is usually the least latency on the hot path — you return to user quickly and label/flag in the background. But this means a potential window where disallowed output is visible; not acceptable for PII/fraud in some compliance regimes. Also you lose the ability to steer generation mid-sequence.
[02:25] Nina (Product): So for PII we probably need synchronous blocking. For policy-based content maybe async is ok. Looking for hybrid patterns.
[02:34] Maya: Exactly. Hybrid designs are common: pre-filter heuristics to catch easy cases, inline filters only for high-risk flows, and async for low-risk routes.
[02:43] [00:03:00] Priya: How does KV cache factor in? If we block mid-generation and backtrack, does that invalidate the cache or cost us extra tokens?
[03:09] Maya: Good question. Our runtime's KV cache is sequence-addressable. If you trigger a safe decode that short-circuits generation and you need to re-generate with a different beam or prompt, you may need to re-warm or replay some tokens, which costs compute and can increase latency. If filter runs purely as a check (no re-generation) and doesn't alter decoding path, it doesn't invalidate KV.
[03:31] Liam: So inline filters that change decoding path are expensive because you lose caching benefits for that session.
[03:36] Maya: Correct. We typically recommend: keep the common-case path cache-friendly, and only invoke regenerative paths for flagged inputs.
[03:44] [00:04:00] Tom: Any numbers on the throughput drop if we colocate filter kernels on GPU vs offload to CPU?
[04:05] Maya: In our internal tests, colocated filters reduced per-token overhead to ~8–12ms additional per check, throughput drop ~12–20% depending on model and batch size. Offloaded CPU checks add variable latency; p95 can double with queueing under load. But these numbers vary by quantization too.
[04:26] Priya: Quantization — do small safety kernels suffer accuracy loss if quantized? We have strict false negative limits.
[04:35] Maya: Short answer: yes, it can. Quantization introduces numeric noise, so classifiers with tight threshold need recalibration. For simple linear probes it's often acceptable with int8 but you should validate on your eval set. Some customers keep safety models in fp16 even when serving main model in int8 to avoid regression.
[04:54] [00:05:00] Avery: Another angle is function/service splitting in VPC: run generation on a private cluster with model bits, but route a copy of the output to a hardened moderation cluster that can run heavier classifiers and logging. That keeps user latency low, but ensures moderation and audit trails. Tradeoff: temporary visibility of content before moderation decisions — may violate policy.
[05:17] Liam: For AtlasPay that transient visibility is OK for some flows but not for payments confirmation or card numbers.
[05:24] Nina: We need zero-exposure for card numbers. So for those flows we need blocking on the hot path.
[05:29] Maya: Then inline or pre-emptive filters are required for those templates. If these flows are templated and low-variance, pre-filter heuristics (regex, deterministic masks) are high value — almost zero latency. Reserve GPU filter only for edge, high-sensitivity fuzzy detections.
[05:47] [00:06:00] Priya: How about batching? If we batch 8 requests to improve utilization, and one request triggers a heavy filter, do we block the batch?
[06:00] Maya: Yes, batching introduces head-of-line blocking. If a heavy check attaches to one request in the batch, whole batch waits. Our runtime supports per-request early-completion in a batch but with complexity: you must split kernels mid-batch which hurts throughput. So design guidance: avoid mixing high-risk and low-risk flows in the same batch class, or use smaller batch sizes for sensitive endpoints.
[06:24] Liam: So maybe have two routes: "fast-path" batched int8 generation with lightweight pre-filters, and "secure-path" smaller batches with inline filters and fp16 models.
[06:35] Maya: Exactly. That's a common pattern. It also plays well with Dedicated or Private deployments where you can assign GPU pools per route.
[06:43] [00:07:00] Tom: On VPC/on-prem, where do we run the audit logs and mod classifiers? We can't send logs outside.
[06:52] Avery: For Private deployments we can deploy the mod service inside the same VPC subnet, behind customer-managed KMS. Audit logs stay in their S3 and don't leave the environment. For extra isolation, some customers run a separate air-gapped moderation stack on a per-region basis.
[07:07] Priya: If we run moderators inside the same host, will that increase vulnerability surface or make compliance reviews harder?
[07:15] Maya: Slightly, but you can harden via RBAC, separate service accounts, and kernel-level cgroups to limit resources. We provide an option to run filters as a different container with strict network egress rules.
[07:28] [00:08:00] Liam: Any good heuristics for deciding token-check frequency? Every token, every 3, or only on punctuation?
[07:39] Maya: It depends on the model and sensitivity. For privacy leaks like card numbers, checking every token or every token that increases digit-run probability makes sense. For policy categories, check on sentence boundaries or when logit spikes for target classes. There's also lightweight fuzzy detectors that run on the prefix with hashing — cheap and catch many cases.
[07:58] Nina: You mentioned logit spikes — can we use token logits directly to trigger filters cheaply?
[08:04] Maya: Yes, it's an efficient signal. Look for high probability tokens matching patterns (like digits) or sudden shifts. That allows cheap gating. But it's model-specific and needs calibration.
[08:14] [00:09:00] Priya: How do these gating decisions show in telemetry? We need to correlate filters with cost.
[08:22] Avery: Our Console exposes token-level breakdowns and per-route cost, including time spent in safety kernels and cache miss rates. We can instrument KV cache hit/miss and tag spans when a safe-decode replay happens so you can attribute cost.
[08:36] Liam: Great. Can we see p99 numbers for pipelines that do inline GPU filters vs async?
[08:42] Maya: We ran a bench: inline colocated kernel p99 increased by ~18–25ms over baseline for medium seqs, async p99 for hot path unchanged but end-to-end detection latency for async was 230–450ms depending on queueing. If you need detection <100ms, inline is required.
[09:02] [00:10:00] Tom: Are there examples of hybrid fail-closed vs fail-open policies? What's recommended?
[09:11] Maya: For regulated data, fail-closed is safest — block outputs if filter subsystem unreachable. For user-facing non-critical content, fail-open with strong logging is common. You can also implement soft-block where you redact and route to human review.
[09:25] Priya: About quantization again — if we quantize the main model to int4/int8 to save cost, but keep filter in fp16, does that create memory pressure?
[09:35] Maya: It can. If your GPU is small, having two model variants increases memory footprint. One approach is to run lightweight filter models on CPU if latency budget allows, or use model sharding where filter weights are loaded on-demand. Tradeoffs.
[09:48] [00:11:00] Avery: Also consider using distilled detectors — these are tiny and can often be run cheaply on the same device as generation. Distillation means some accuracy loss, but for gating it's often acceptable.
[09:59] Liam: Can you speak to the impact on billing cost if we add inline checks to all requests? Ballpark percentage increase?
[10:07] Maya: Ballpark — adding colocated inline checks can increase GPU compute cost 10–30% depending on model and check frequency. If you offload to CPU, you might increase infra cost but not GPU cost; overall cost delta depends on your instance pricing. We'll provide a model-specific estimate in the follow-up spreadsheet.
[10:25] [00:12:00] Nina: For pilot, we want to try three routes: template-sensitive card flows (fail-closed inline), support chat (async post-gen), and auth flows (pre-filter heuristics). Can you outline a test plan?
[10:37] Avery: Yes. We'll: 1) run microbench marks for each pattern with your peak qps; 2) measure p95/p99, KV hit rates, and added cost; 3) run a small user-sim with warm and cold caches to see tail. We'll share results and recommended configuration.
[10:56] [00:13:00] Priya: For the microbench, what data do you need from us?
[11:02] Maya: Peak qps, session lengths, typical prompt prefixes, and retention window for KV (how long you keep session keys). Also security constraints (no external egress), and model family you want us to test with.
[11:14] Priya: We'll send that by Monday.
[11:18] [00:14:00] Maya: One more note — batching and KV warmups: when you have many short sessions, batching helps but you need to ensure your cache hit ratio remains high. Techniques: sticky routing to prefer warmed replicas, adaptive batching where low latency routes get minimum batching. That reduces the penalty for inline checks.
[11:36] Liam: Sticky routing meaning map session to same worker?
[11:40] Maya: Yes, which keeps KV state warm on that worker and avoids replaying tokens. It's effective but reduces scheduling flexibility.
[11:46] [00:15:00] Tom: Anything else on audit/compliance?
[11:49] Avery: We support write-once audit logs to customer-managed object store, and can redact logs at ingestion for PII. Also provide signed attestations for model versions and filter rule-sets.
[11:59] Nina: Good. We'll want the attestations for our SOC review.
[12:03] [00:16:00] Maya: Quick real-world note: one customer tried to do full inline filtering for everything, and throughput dropped 40% and cost spiked. They switched to hybrid: deterministic pre-filters + inline for top 2% high-risk, async for the rest. That balanced cost and risk.
[12:21] Priya: Helpful.
[12:23] [00:17:00] Liam: On false positives — if inline filter false positives are high, that will hurt UX. How do we tune?
[12:31] Maya: You need a labeled eval set and incremental rollouts. Canary at low traffic with logging (don't block, just log) to gather precision/recall, then progressively tighten thresholds. Our Console supports per-rule evaluation dashboards.
[12:44] [00:18:00] Avery: Let's talk implementation options inside the Private deployment: run filters as a sidecar in the same pod, as a co-located in-process library, or as a central moderation cluster. Sidecar gives isolation and control; in-process gives lowest latency; central cluster gives easiest scaling. Pick based on sensitivity and ops capacity.
[13:07] Nina: Ops capacity is limited for us, so sidecar seems heavy. Could we do in-process for a few key endpoints and central cluster for the rest?
[13:14] Maya: Absolutely, that hybrid is normal.
[13:18] [00:19:00] Priya: Any gotchas with Kubernetes or container runtime that would affect KV cache persistence across pod restarts?
[13:26] Maya: KV cache in our runtime is in-memory per worker; pod restart causes cold cache. For sticky routing you should make sure pod churn is low during peak or add external persistent KV store to rehydrate. But persistent KV across workers is more complex and has consistency tradeoffs.
[13:44] Liam: Okay. Seems like next step is the benchmark and our usage numbers.
[13:49] Avery: Yup. We'll run the A/B (inline vs async) and give you p50/p95/p99 and cost. Also include the hybrid suggested configs.
[13:57] [00:20:00] Tom: Final question — can we get a demo of Console showing token-level cost traces?
[14:05] Avery: Yes, we'll schedule a Console walkthrough with your security folks.
[14:09] Nina: Thanks.
[14:11] [00:21:00] Closing remarks and quick recap of next steps.
